title: Per Cent Grid
context: Grade 5, the first pages on per cent. An adult sees a new sign. What the pages are doing is counting out of a hundred: a per cent is the number of cells shaded when the whole is cut into one hundred equal cells. Any cells of the right number are correct, and a strip of ten equal cells is the same idea in columns.

writeup.why: Read and shade a per cent on a hundred grid as a count out of a hundred, write it as a fraction over 100 and with the % sign, and see a strip of ten equal cells as the same whole in columns.
writeup.look: A full ten by ten grid at the left, the Columns and cells counter under it, a fraction card and a per cent card at its right, and on the last phase a strip of ten equal cells.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Per Cent Grid' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many cells are shaded, out of one hundred. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The grid is 480 by 480 with its top left at x 110, y 230, ruled into ten columns and ten rows of equal cells in near-black and labelled Whole and 100% above it. Shaded cells are deep blue and unshaded cells stay warm white. The Columns and cells counter stands at x 640, y 240, reading the shading in words as full columns and single cells. The fraction card and the per cent card stand one above the other at x 640, y 360 and x 640, y 480, each 300 by 90, and turn green when the child's answer matches the shading. The Scatter and Fold buttons sit side by side at x 640, y 620, each labelled in words. On the fourth phase the ten columns close up into a strip 900 long and 80 tall at x 110, y 420, each of its ten equal cells labelled one tenth, the shaded columns becoming shaded cells. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a fraction bar key and a % key, for setting a count of cells up to one hundred, or typing a fraction or a per cent into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. The part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, labelled Given. The per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, and what is left after a part is used, is green, labelled Answer or Left. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion, labelled Both terms or Times 100. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet, labelled Unit fact. The part used, taken away or not won is rose, labelled Used or Not won. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey, labelled Place holder, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the % sign is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The cards show the last shading as a fraction over 100 and as a per cent, with the grid and its folded strip side by side.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, the moment Fold is tapped, the ten columns glide together into one long strip, the shaded columns staying shaded, and the per cent card does not change at all.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase the full ten by ten grid sits at the left with some columns and cells already shaded deep blue, and the fraction and per cent cards blank. On the second the question card shows a fraction over one hundred beside an empty grid. On the third the grid is empty and the question card asks for a per cent. On the fourth the ten columns of the grid are outlined in amber and the Fold button waits. One thing moves, once: the first cell, or the Fold button on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any shading of the grid, scattered or in columns, and the grid folded into its strip and back. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on counting out of a hundred, fractions over a hundred, shading a per cent and the strip of ten.

source_tool.description: A full ten by ten grid, 480 by 480, sits at the left of the working area, labelled Whole and 100%, with its ten columns ruled in near-black and every cell the same size. Dragging across cells shades them deep blue; dragging back clears them. A Columns and cells counter under the grid reads the shading as full columns of ten and single cells. A fraction card and a per cent card to the right give the shading as a number over 100 and as that number with the % sign, turning green when the child's answer matches. A Scatter button moves the shaded cells to other places on the grid while their number stays the same, and the cards stay as they were. On the last phase a Fold button slides the ten columns together into one strip of ten equal cells, each cell one column of the grid, labelled 1 tenth. A number pad sets any count from zero to one hundred, or types a fraction or a per cent. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many cells are shaded.
source_tool.art_direction: Squared paper on a classroom desk / Picture book

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, strips cut into equal cells, fraction bars with their denominator of one hundred built beside them, measuring jugs, tapes and scales with their units written on them.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip of ten has ten cells of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
A whole is always labelled 100%, so the child sees what one hundred per cent means before any part is named.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance: full columns of ten first, then single cells.
A product that becomes a per cent is always written with its brackets, and the % sign comes last. A decimal reaches a per cent through its hundredths, never by moving anything.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: cells filling a grid, both terms of a fraction growing together, a unit fact rewriting an amount, or a used part lifting away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a cell or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a per cent plays in a piece of working: the part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, and the per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, with what is left after a part is used, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet. The part used, taken away or not won is rose. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the % sign itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Both terms, Unit fact, Used, Not won, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.

voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the full columns first, then the single cells.
voice.onNext: A new grid. Every cell is one hundredth.
voice.opening: A hundred equal cells, waiting to be shaded.
voice.onFinish: You counted out of a hundred every time.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Shade, scatter and fold as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

phase_map.concept: Per cent means out of a hundred

placement.where: After the class has drawn a hundred grid on squared paper and shaded some columns. The tool is what moves the shading about without changing its count, and what folds the columns into a strip, which paper cannot do in front of the child.

answer_key.rule: Per cent means out of a hundred. A hundred grid has 100 equal cells, so each cell is one hundredth, and a number of shaded cells over 100 is that many per cent. A fraction over 100 is written as a per cent by its numerator, with the % sign. To show a per cent, shade that many cells: full columns of ten first, then single cells, and which cells does not matter, only how many. A strip of ten equal cells is the whole, 100%. Each of its cells is one tenth of it, ten hundredths. A percentage is an amount written as a per cent.
answer_key.wrong: The grid is shown again with the shaded cells counted column by column, a number on each full column and on each single cell, and the child's answer is shaded on a second grid beside it, so the two counts are seen side by side. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The grid has 100 equal cells, so each cell is one hundredth.
63 of the 100 cells are shaded, so 63/100 of the grid is shaded.
Per cent means out of a hundred, so 63/100 is 63%.
items.question: A hundred grid has 100 equal cells, and 63 of them are shaded. What per cent of the grid is shaded?
items.checkpoint: Per cent means out of a hundred.
items.misconception: Giving 37%, which counts the cells left unshaded instead of the cells shaded.

steps: The numerator counts the hundredths, so 71/100 is 71 hundredths.
Per cent means out of a hundred, so 71 hundredths is 71%.
items.question: Write 71/100 as a per cent.
items.checkpoint: The numerator of a fraction over 100 is the per cent.
items.misconception: Writing 71 with no % sign, which would mean 71 wholes rather than 71 hundredths.

steps: Any 34 cells will do: which cells does not matter, only how many.
items.question: Shade 34% of a hundred grid.
items.checkpoint: Count full columns of ten first, then single cells.
items.misconception: Shading four full columns and three more cells, 43 in all, which swaps the columns and the single cells.

steps: Each cell is one tenth of the strip, and one tenth is 10 hundredths.
3 cells are 3 lots of 10%, which is 30%.
items.question: A strip is cut into 10 equal cells, and 3 of them are shaded. What per cent of the strip is shaded?
items.checkpoint: Each cell of a strip of ten equal cells is one tenth of the whole.
items.misconception: Saying 3%, which counts each cell as one hundredth as if the strip had a hundred cells.

items.question: How many cells of a hundred grid do you shade to show 16%?

items.final_answer: 94%, because 9 columns are 90 cells and 4 more make 94 of the 100

items.question: Two children show 38% on hundred grids. One shades three full columns and 8 more cells. The other shades 38 cells scattered about. Who is right?
items.final_answer: Both are right. Each shaded 38 of the 100 cells, and which cells does not matter

teaching_notes: Shade a hundred grid on squared paper before the tool opens, and say per cent means out of a hundred every time the sign is written. Count full columns of ten first and single cells after. Any cells of the right count are correct, so accept a scattered shading as readily as a tidy one. Fold a paper strip of ten equal cells beside the grid so each cell is seen to be one column. A percentage is an amount written as a per cent. Use fresh numbers: the exercise's fractions are the child's to shade.
generation_prompt: Build a per cent tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A full ten by ten grid, 480 by 480, sits at the left of the working area, labelled Whole and 100%. Dragging shades cells deep blue. A Columns and cells counter reads the shading as full columns and single cells, and a fraction card and a per cent card give it as a number over 100 and with the % sign, turning green when the answer matches. A Scatter button moves the shaded cells without changing their number. On the last phase a Fold button slides the ten columns together into a strip of ten equal cells, each labelled 1 tenth. A number pad sets a count of cells or types a fraction or a per cent. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of shaded cells. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right.
